Lines go to standard error unless log_to_stdout(true) is called. Messages below the level are dropped.

**Constants**

- `LOG_DEBUG = 10`
- `LOG_INFO = 20`
- `LOG_WARN = 30`
- `LOG_ERROR = 40`
- `LOG_OFF = 100`

**Functions**

- `fn log_set_level(level: int)` - messages below this level (LOG_DEBUG, LOG_INFO, LOG_WARN, LOG_ERROR, LOG_OFF) are dropped
- `fn log_get_level() -> int` - the level as set by log_set_level
- `fn log_level_from_name(name: str) -> int?` - the level for a name: "debug", "info", "warn" (or "warning"), "error", "off"; nil for anything else
- `fn log_set_file(path: str) -> bool` - also appends every logged line to this file ("" stops that); false when the file cannot be written
- `fn log_timestamps(on: bool)` - puts the local date and time in front of every line
- `fn log_to_stdout(on: bool)` - writes to standard output instead of standard error
- `fn log_set_prefix(prefix: str)` - text put after the level on every line, for example the program name: "[mytool] "
- `fn log_level_name(level: int) -> str` - the name of a level: "DEBUG", "INFO", "WARN", "ERROR"
- `fn log_at(level: int, msg: str)` - logs msg at the given level (the other log_* functions call this)
- `fn log_debug(msg: str)`
- `fn log_info(msg: str)`
- `fn log_warn(msg: str)`
- `fn log_error(msg: str)`

## std/math

Number theory helpers (like Python's math) and descriptive statistics (like Python's statistics).

```text
import "std/math"
math_factorial(10)                  == 3628800
math_is_prime(97)                   == true
math_primes(20)                     == [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]
stats_mean([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])    == 2.5
stats_stdev([2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0]) == 2.0
```

The statistics functions take [float] and panic on an empty array (and the sample versions on fewer than 2 values).

**Functions**

- `fn math_factorial(n: int) -> int` - n! as an int; panics for a negative n and for n > 20 (the result would not fit in 64 bits)
- `fn math_binomial(n: int, k: int) -> int` - n choose k (the number of ways to pick k of n); 0 when k is outside 0..n
- `fn math_isqrt(n: int) -> int` - the largest int r with r * r <= n; panics for a negative n
- `fn math_is_prime(n: int) -> bool` - true when n is a prime number (trial division, fine up to about 10^12)
- `fn math_primes(limit: int) -> [int]` - all primes <= limit, smallest first (sieve of Eratosthenes)
- `fn math_prime_factors(n: int) -> [int]` - the prime factors of n with repeats, smallest first: math_prime_factors(12) == [2, 2, 3]; [] for n < 2
- `fn math_fib(n: int) -> int` - the n-th Fibonacci number (fib(0) == 0, fib(1) == 1); panics when n < 0 or n > 92 (it would overflow)
- `fn math_mod_pow(base: int, exp: int, m: int) -> int` - (base ** exp) % m without overflow for m up to 3 billion; exp must not be negative
- `fn math_lerp(a: float, b: float, t: float) -> float` - a + (b - a) * t: the point t of the way from a to b (t = 0.5 is the middle)
- `fn stats_sum(a: [float]) -> float` - the sum of the values
- `fn stats_mean(a: [float]) -> float` - the average
- `fn stats_median(a: [float]) -> float` - the middle value (the average of the two middle values when the count is even)
- `fn stats_mode<T>(a: [T]) -> T` - the most common value (the first one that reaches the highest count on ties)
- `fn stats_variance(a: [float]) -> float` - population variance (divides by n)
- `fn stats_sample_variance(a: [float]) -> float` - sample variance (divides by n - 1); needs at least 2 values
- `fn stats_stdev(a: [float]) -> float` - population standard deviation
- `fn stats_sample_stdev(a: [float]) -> float` - sample standard deviation
- `fn stats_percentile(a: [float], p: float) -> float` - the p-th percentile (p from 0 to 100) with linear interpolation between neighbours: stats_percentile(a, 50.0) is the median
- `fn stats_correlation(a: [float], b: [float]) -> float` - the Pearson correlation of two arrays of the same length (nan when one of them is constant)

## std/net

TCP connections: a client (tcp_connect) and a server (tcp_listen), built on the Windows socket library.

```text
import "std/net"

match tcp_connect("example.com", 80) {
    Result.Ok(c) => {
        c.write("HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n")
        println(c.read_line() ?? "no answer")      // HTTP/1.0 200 OK
        c.close()
    }
    Result.Err(e) => println("cannot connect: " + e)
}

let server = tcp_listen(0).unwrap()     // port 0 picks a free port: server.port
let client = server.accept().unwrap()   // waits for the next connection
```

Reads wait at most `timeout_ms` (30 seconds unless changed with set_timeout); a read that times out
returns nil, the same as a closed connection. Data is bytes in a str.

**Types**

a connection to another program

```text
struct TcpConn {
    sock: int
    pending: str        // bytes already received but not yet returned
}
```

a server waiting for connections

```text
struct TcpServer {
    sock: int
    port: int           // the port it listens on (useful after tcp_listen(0))
}
```


**Functions**

- `fn net_start()`
- `fn net_error_text(code: int) -> str` - a readable message for a Windows socket error code
- `fn net_last_error() -> str`
- `fn net_lookup(host: str, port: int, passive: bool) -> Result<int, str>` - looks up a host and port; returns the addrinfo list (free it with net_freeaddrinfo) or an error
- `fn net_resolve(host: str) -> [str]` - the IPv4 addresses of a host name, like ["93.184.215.14"]; empty when it cannot be found
- `fn tcp_connect(host: str, port: int, timeout_ms: int = 10000) -> Result<TcpConn, str>` - connects to host:port; waits at most timeout_ms for the other side to answer
- `fn tcp_listen(port: int, host: str = "127.0.0.1") -> Result<TcpServer, str>` - listens on a port; host "" listens on every network, "127.0.0.1" (the default) only on this computer

**Methods of `TcpConn`**

- `.set_timeout(ms: int)` - how long a read (and a write) may wait, in milliseconds; 0 waits forever
- `.write(data: str) -> bool` - sends all of data; false when the connection is broken
- `.write_line(line: str) -> bool` - sends data followed by "\r\n"
- `.raw_read(max: int) -> str?`
- `.read(max: int = 65536) -> str?` - the next bytes that arrive (at most max); nil when the connection is closed or the read timed out
- `.read_line() -> str?` - the next line without its "\n" (or "\r\n"); nil when nothing is left
- `.read_exact(n: int) -> str?` - exactly n bytes; nil when the connection closes first
- `.read_all() -> str` - everything until the other side closes the connection
- `.close_write()` - tells the other side that nothing more will be sent (reading still works)
- `.close()` - closes the connection

**Methods of `TcpServer`**

- `.accept() -> Result<TcpConn, str>` - waits for the next connection
- `.close()` - stops listening

## std/path

Working with file paths as text (no file system access).

```text
import "std/path"
path_join("a", "b.txt")            == "a\\b.txt"
path_basename("C:\\x\\y.tar.gz")   == "y.tar.gz"
path_dirname("C:\\x\\y.txt")       == "C:\\x"
path_ext("notes.md")               == ".md"
path_stem("notes.md")              == "notes"
path_normalize("a/./b/../c")       == "a\\c"
```

Both / and \ are accepted as separators on input. Results use \ (the Windows separator).

**Functions**

- `fn path_is_sep(c: byte) -> bool`
- `fn path_last_sep(p: str) -> int` - index of the last separator in p, or -1
- `fn path_basename(p: str) -> str` - the last part of the path: path_basename("a\\b\\c.txt") == "c.txt"
- `fn path_dirname(p: str) -> str` - everything before the last part: path_dirname("a\\b\\c.txt") == "a\\b"; "" when there is no folder part
- `fn path_ext(p: str) -> str` - the extension of the last part including the dot, or "": path_ext("a.tar.gz") == ".gz"
- `fn path_stem(p: str) -> str` - the last part without its extension: path_stem("a\\b.txt") == "b"
- `fn path_with_ext(p: str, ext: str) -> str` - the path with another extension (give it with the dot, or "" to remove it)
- `fn path_is_absolute(p: str) -> bool` - true for "C:\\x", "\\\\server\\share" and "\\x"
- `fn path_join(a: str, b: str) -> str` - joins parts with one separator between them; an absolute part restarts the path
- `fn path_join_all(parts: [str]) -> str` - joins any number of parts: path_join_all(["a", "b", "c"]) == "a\\b\\c"
- `fn path_parts(p: str) -> [str]` - splits into parts at the separators; empty parts are dropped
- `fn path_normalize(p: str) -> str` - removes "." parts, resolves ".." where it can and uses \ everywhere: path_normalize("a/./b/../c") == "a\\c"

## std/process

Running programs and capturing what they print, environment variables, process info.

```text
import "std/process"
let r = proc_output("cmd /c echo hi")
println(r.0, r.1)                     // 0 "hi\r\n"
proc_setenv("MODE", "fast")
println(proc_pid(), proc_cpu_count())
```

run_command and run_process (the prelude) run a program with its output on the console;
proc_output and proc_output_args capture it as text instead.

**Functions**

- `fn proc_output(cmdline: str) -> (int, str)` - Runs a command line, waits for it and returns (exit code, everything it wrote to stdout and stderr). The exit code is -1 and the text empty when the program could not be started.
- `fn proc_output_args(path: str, args: [str]) -> (int, str)` - like proc_output, for a program and its arguments (they are quoted for you)
- `fn proc_setenv(name: str, value: str) -> bool` - sets an environment variable for this program and the programs it starts; false when that fails
- `fn proc_unsetenv(name: str) -> bool` - removes an environment variable
- `fn proc_pid() -> int` - the id of this process
- `fn proc_cpu_count() -> int` - the number of logical processors

## std/random

More random numbers, like Python's random module (the prelude has rand_int, rand_float, rand_choice, shuffle).

```text
import "std/random"
random_range(0, 10)                   // 0..9, like Python's randrange (the end is not included)
random_range(0, 100, 5)               // 0, 5, 10 ... 95
random_sample([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)     // 2 different elements
random_choices(["a", "b"], 5)         // 5 elements, repeats allowed
random_weighted(["rare", "common"], [1.0, 9.0])
random_gauss(100.0, 15.0)             // normally distributed
random_uuid()                         // "3f2b8c1e-...-4..."
```

All of them use the same generator as rand_int, so rand_seed(n) makes a run repeatable.

**Functions**

- `fn random_range(lo: int, hi: int, by: int = 1) -> int` - a random number from lo up to (not including) hi, moving in steps of by: random_range(0, 10, 3) is 0, 3, 6 or 9
- `fn random_bool(p: float = 0.5) -> bool` - true with probability p (0.5 by default)
- `fn random_gauss(mean: float = 0.0, sd: float = 1.0) -> float` - a normally distributed number with the given mean and standard deviation (Box-Muller)
- `fn random_sample<T>(a: [T], k: int) -> [T]` - k different elements of a, in random order (a itself is not changed); k must not be larger than a.len()
- `fn random_choices<T>(a: [T], k: int) -> [T]` - k elements of a picked one by one, so the same element can come up again; a must not be empty
- `fn random_weighted<T>(a: [T], weights: [float]) -> T` - one element of a, where weights[i] (not negative, not all 0) says how likely a[i] is compared to the others
- `fn random_shuffled<T>(a: [T]) -> [T]` - a shuffled copy of a (shuffle changes the array itself)
- `fn random_string(n: int, alphabet: str = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789") -> str` - n random characters from the alphabet (letters and digits by default)
- `fn random_hex(n: int) -> str` - 2 * n lowercase hex digits from n random bytes
- `fn random_uuid() -> str` - a random (version 4) UUID like "9b2f4c1e-7d3a-4f8e-a1b2-0c9d8e7f6a5b"

## std/regex

Regular expressions (a backtracking matcher working on bytes).

```text
import "std/regex"
let re = regex_compile("(\\d+)-(\\d+)").unwrap()
if let m = re.find("tel 12-345") { println(m.text, m.group(1), m.group(2), m.start) }   // 12-345 12 345 4
println(re.is_match("no digits"))                          // false
println(re.replace_all("1-2 and 3-4", "$2:$1"))            // 2:1 and 4:3
println(regex_split(",\\s*", "a, b,c"))                    // ["a", "b", "c"]
```

Supported: literals, . (any byte except newline), classes [a-z0-9_] and [^...], \d \w \s and their
upper-case negations, \b \B, anchors ^ $, groups (...) and (?:...), alternation a|b, and the
repeats * + ? {n} {n,} {n,m} (add ? after one for the lazy form). Escape a special character with \.
Not supported: look-around, back-references and named groups.
Text is matched byte by byte, so . matches one byte of a multi-byte character.

**Types**

```text
struct RxNode {
    kind: int          // 0 char, 1 any, 2 set, 3 sequence, 4 alternation, 5 repeat, 6 group, 7 start, 8 end, 9 word edge, 10 not word edge, 11 empty
    ch: int            // the byte of a char node, the number of a group node
    set: [bool]
    kids: [RxNode]
    min: int
    max: int           // -1 means no limit
    lazy: bool
}
```

a compiled regular expression

```text
struct Regex {
    pattern: str
    root: RxNode
    groups: int        // number of capture groups
}
```

one match: the byte range [start, end), its text and the text of every group (index 0 is the whole match, "" for a group that did not take part)

```text
struct RxMatch {
    start: int
    end: int
    text: str
    groups: [str]
}
```

```text
struct RxParser {
    p: str
    i: int
    ngroups: int
    err: str
    icase: bool
}
```

```text
struct RxState {
    s: str
    caps: [int]
    end: int
}
```


**Functions**

- `fn rx_node(kind: int) -> RxNode`
- `fn rx_is_word(c: int) -> bool`
- `fn rx_class_set(c: byte) -> [bool]`
- `fn rx_escape_byte(c: byte) -> int`
- `fn rx_fail(ps: RxParser, msg: str)`
- `fn rx_peek(ps: RxParser) -> int`
- `fn rx_icase_set(set: [bool])`
- `fn rx_char_node(ps: RxParser, c: int) -> RxNode`
- `fn rx_parse_class(ps: RxParser) -> RxNode`
- `fn rx_parse_atom(ps: RxParser) -> RxNode`
- `fn rx_parse_braces(ps: RxParser, n: RxNode) -> bool` - reads {n}, {n,} or {n,m} at ps.i (which is on the {); returns false and leaves ps.i alone when it is not one
- `fn rx_parse_seq(ps: RxParser) -> RxNode`
- `fn rx_parse_alt(ps: RxParser) -> RxNode`
- `fn regex_compile(pattern: str, ignore_case: bool = false) -> Result<Regex, str>` - Compiles a pattern. The error text says what is wrong and where. With ignore_case, letters match in both cases.
- `fn regex(pattern: str, ignore_case: bool = false) -> Regex` - the compiled pattern; panics when it is not valid
- `fn rx_one(n: RxNode, s: str, i: int) -> bool`
- `fn rx_accept(st: RxState, j: int) -> bool`
- `fn rx_seq(kids: [RxNode], idx: int, st: RxState, i: int, k: fn(int) -> bool) -> bool`
- `fn rx_rep(n: RxNode, st: RxState, i: int, count: int, k: fn(int) -> bool) -> bool`
- `fn rx_m(n: RxNode, st: RxState, i: int, k: fn(int) -> bool) -> bool`
- `fn rx_find_at(re: Regex, s: str, from: int) -> RxMatch?`
- `fn regex_anchored(re: Regex, s: str) -> bool` - true when some match of re covers the whole of s (tries the pattern at 0 with a required end)
- `fn rx_expand(repl: str, m: RxMatch) -> str`
- `fn regex_match(pattern: str, s: str) -> bool` - true when the pattern matches somewhere in s; panics when the pattern is not valid
- `fn regex_split(pattern: str, s: str) -> [str]` - the pieces of s between the matches of the pattern; panics when the pattern is not valid
- `fn regex_replace(pattern: str, s: str, repl: str) -> str` - replaces every match of the pattern in s (see Regex.replace for $1); panics when the pattern is not valid
- `fn regex_find_all(pattern: str, s: str) -> [str]` - the text of every match of the pattern in s; panics when the pattern is not valid

**Methods of `RxMatch`**

- `.group(i: int) -> str` - the text of group i (0 is the whole match); "" when there is no such group

**Methods of `Regex`**

- `.find(s: str) -> RxMatch?` - the first match in s, or nil
- `.find_from(s: str, from: int) -> RxMatch?` - the first match that starts at byte position from or later, or nil
- `.is_match(s: str) -> bool` - true when the pattern matches somewhere in s
- `.full_match(s: str) -> bool` - true when the pattern matches the whole of s
- `.find_all(s: str) -> [RxMatch]` - all the matches, left to right, not overlapping
- `.replace(s: str, repl: str) -> str` - replaces the first match; in repl, $0 is the whole match, $1 to $9 are groups and $$ is a dollar sign
- `.replace_all(s: str, repl: str) -> str` - replaces every match (see replace for $1)
- `.replace_with(s: str, f: fn(RxMatch) -> str) -> str` - replaces every match with whatever f returns for it
- `.split(s: str) -> [str]` - the pieces of s between the matches

## std/test

A small test framework for ATF programs.

```text
import "std/test"

fn main() -> int {
    test("addition", || {
        expect_eq(1 + 1, 2)
        expect(2 > 1, "two is bigger")
    })
    test("a panic is a failure", || { expect_eq([1, 2][0], 1) })
    expect_panics("division by zero", || { let z = 0; println(1 / z) })
    return test_report()          // prints a summary, returns 0 when everything passed (else 1)
}
```

A failed expectation is recorded and the test goes on; a panic inside a test fails that test
and the next test still runs. Every test prints one line, "ok" or "FAIL" followed by the reasons.

**Functions**

- `fn test_fail(msg: str)` - records a failure for the running test
- `fn test(name: str, f: fn())` - Runs f as a test called name and prints "ok   name" or "FAIL name" with the reasons.
- `fn expect(cond: bool, msg: str = "expectation failed")` - fails the test when cond is false
- `fn expect_eq<T>(got: T, want: T)` - fails the test when got != want, showing both values
- `fn expect_ne<T>(got: T, other: T)` - fails the test when got == other
- `fn expect_near(got: float, want: float, eps: float = 0.000001)` - fails the test when two floats differ by more than eps
- `fn expect_panics(name: str, f: fn())` - Runs f as a test called name that passes only when f panics.
- `fn test_report() -> int` - prints how many tests ran and failed; returns 0 when all passed and 1 otherwise (use it as the exit code of main)

## std/text

Text helpers known from Python (textwrap, string, str methods) and other languages.

```text
import "std/text"
text_title("hello big world")          == "Hello Big World"
text_snake_case("HelloBigWorld")       == "hello_big_world"
text_wrap("the quick brown fox", 10)   == ["the quick", "brown fox"]
text_template("Hi ${name}!", {"name": "Ana"}) == "Hi Ana!"
print(text_table([["name", "age"], ["Ana", "7"]]))
```

Text is bytes: the case functions change only ASCII letters, and widths count bytes.

**Functions**

- `fn text_is_lower_byte(c: byte) -> bool`
- `fn text_is_upper_byte(c: byte) -> bool`
- `fn text_is_alnum_byte(c: byte) -> bool`
- `fn text_is_alpha(s: str) -> bool` - true when the text is not empty and every byte is an ASCII letter
- `fn text_is_alnum(s: str) -> bool` - true when the text is not empty and every byte is an ASCII letter or digit
- `fn text_title(s: str) -> str` - the first letter of every word in uppercase and the others in lowercase: "hello big world" -> "Hello Big World"
- `fn text_swapcase(s: str) -> str` - upper case letters become lower case and the other way round
- `fn text_partition(s: str, sep: str) -> (str, str, str)` - splits at the first sep: (before, sep, after); (s, "", "") when sep is not found
- `fn text_rpartition(s: str, sep: str) -> (str, str, str)` - splits at the last sep: (before, sep, after); ("", "", s) when sep is not found
- `fn text_split_n(s: str, sep: str, max_splits: int) -> [str]` - like split, but cuts at most max_splits times (the rest stays in the last piece): text_split_n("a=b=c", "=", 1) == ["a", "b=c"]
- `fn text_words(s: str) -> [str]` - the words of a name written in any style: "HelloBigWorld", "hello_big-world" and "hello big world" give ["hello", "big", "world"]
- `fn text_snake_case(s: str) -> str` - "HelloBigWorld" -> "hello_big_world"
- `fn text_kebab_case(s: str) -> str` - "HelloBigWorld" -> "hello-big-world"
- `fn text_camel_case(s: str) -> str` - "hello_big_world" -> "helloBigWorld"
- `fn text_pascal_case(s: str) -> str` - "hello_big_world" -> "HelloBigWorld"
- `fn text_wrap(s: str, width: int) -> [str]` - Breaks the text into lines of at most width bytes at the spaces (a longer word gets a line of its own). Runs of whitespace count as one space; empty text gives [].
- `fn text_fill(s: str, width: int) -> str` - text_wrap joined with newlines
- `fn text_indent(s: str, prefix: str) -> str` - prefix added in front of every non-empty line
- `fn text_dedent(s: str) -> str` - removes the leading whitespace that all non-empty lines have in common
- `fn text_shorten(s: str, width: int, placeholder: str = "...") -> str` - the text cut to at most width bytes, ending in placeholder when it had to be cut: text_shorten("hello world", 8) == "hello..."
- `fn text_distance(a: str, b: str) -> int` - the number of single-byte edits (insert, delete, change) that turn a into b - handy for "did you mean ...?"
- `fn text_template(s: str, values: {str: str}) -> str` - Replaces ${name} (or $name) by the value in values, like Python's string.Template. A name that is missing stays as written; $$ gives a single $.
- `fn text_table(rows: [[str]], right: bool = false) -> str` - Rows of cells as a text table: every column as wide as its widest cell, columns separated by two spaces, no trailing spaces, every line ends with a newline. Numbers look better aligned right: pass right: true.

## std/toml

Reading and writing TOML (the configuration file format).

```text
import "std/toml"

let r = toml_parse("name = \"app\"\n[server]\nport = 8080\nhosts = [\"a\", \"b\"]\n")
match r {
    Result.Ok(v) => println(v.get_str("name", "?"), v.query("server.port"), v.query("server.hosts[1]"))
    Result.Err(e) => println("bad toml: " + e)          // e.g. "line 3: expected '=' after the key"
}
println(toml_stringify(doc))
```

A document becomes a JsonValue (from std/json, which this module imports): tables are objects,
arrays are arrays, integers are Int, floats are Float. Dates and times are kept as Str.
Supported: comments, bare / quoted / dotted keys, [tables], [[arrays of tables]], inline tables,
multi-line arrays, basic and literal strings (also the multi-line forms), numbers with _ and 0x 0o 0b.
Not supported: inf and nan values.

**Types**

```text
struct TomlParser {
    s: str
    i: int
    err: str
}
```


**Functions**

- `fn toml_line_of(p: TomlParser) -> int`
- `fn toml_fail(p: TomlParser, msg: str)`
- `fn toml_peek(p: TomlParser) -> int`
- `fn toml_at(p: TomlParser, t: str) -> bool`
- `fn toml_skip_ws(p: TomlParser)` - skips spaces and tabs
- `fn toml_skip_comment(p: TomlParser)` - skips to the end of a comment (not past the newline)
- `fn toml_skip_blank(p: TomlParser)` - skips spaces, comments and newlines
- `fn toml_utf8(sb: StrBuilder, cp: int)`
- `fn toml_hex_value(p: TomlParser, digits: int) -> int`
- `fn toml_parse_string(p: TomlParser) -> str` - a string starting at the opening quote; handles """ ''' and the one-line forms
- `fn toml_is_bare(c: int) -> bool`
- `fn toml_parse_key_part(p: TomlParser) -> str` - one key part: bare, "quoted" or 'literal'
- `fn toml_parse_key(p: TomlParser) -> [str]` - a dotted key such as a.b."c d"
- `fn toml_looks_like_date(tok: str) -> bool`
- `fn toml_parse_scalar(p: TomlParser) -> JsonValue`
- `fn toml_parse_value(p: TomlParser) -> JsonValue`
- `fn toml_object_of(v: JsonValue) -> {str: JsonValue}?`
- `fn toml_descend(p: TomlParser, m: {str: JsonValue}, key: str) -> {str: JsonValue}` - the table named key inside m (created when missing); an array of tables gives its last table
- `fn toml_set(p: TomlParser, m: {str: JsonValue}, key: [str], v: JsonValue)`
- `fn toml_end_of_line(p: TomlParser)`
- `fn toml_parse(text: str) -> Result<JsonValue, str>` - Reads a TOML document. The error text starts with the line number.
- `fn toml_quote(s: str) -> str`
- `fn toml_key_text(k: str) -> str`
- `fn toml_is_table_array(v: JsonValue) -> bool`
- `fn toml_inline(v: JsonValue) -> str`
- `fn toml_inline_table(o: {str: JsonValue}) -> str`
- `fn toml_float(f: float) -> str`
- `fn toml_write_table(sb: StrBuilder, o: {str: JsonValue}, path: [str])`
- `fn toml_stringify(v: JsonValue) -> str` - Writes a document (a JsonValue object) as TOML text. Plain values come first in each table, then its sub-tables. Null values are written as empty strings, since TOML has no null. Panics when v is not an object.

## std/ui

Windows, layout and styling for graphical programs (Windows).

```text
import "std/ui"

struct App { count: int = 0 }

fn view(app: App) -> Node {
    return column([
        text("Clicked {app.count} times").font_size(22).bold(),
        button("Click me", || { app.count += 1 }).bg(hex("#2563eb")).color(WHITE),
    ]).padding(24).gap(12).center()
}

fn main() {
    let app = App()
    ui_run("Counter", 420, 260, || view(app))
}
```

The idea is the one of HTML + CSS, written as ATF code:
```text
- the screen is a tree of Node values built by a view function (column, row, text, button, ...)
- every Node takes CSS-like style methods that chain: .padding(8, 16) .bg(..) .radius(12) .shadow(..)
- layout is flexbox: rows and columns with gap, align, justify, grow, wrap, plus grid and absolute positions
- reusable styles are values:  let card = style().bg(WHITE).radius(16)   then  .style(card)
  styles combine with +  (card + raised), and have states: .hover(style()...) .pressed(..) .focused(..)
- text styles (color, font_size, bold, ...) are inherited by the children, like in CSS
- after every event (click, typing, timer) the view function runs again and the window is redrawn,
  so the program only changes its own data; there is no need to update widgets by hand
```
Colors are ints 0xAARRGGBB: hex("#2563eb"), rgb(37, 99, 235), rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3), WHITE, BLACK, TRANSPARENT.
Lengths are in pixels at 100% screen scale; they are scaled for high-DPI screens automatically.
Every method of Style also works directly on a Node:  text("Hi").bold().color(WHITE).padding(8)
Without a window (tests, docs): ui_screenshot(view, w, h, "shot.bmp"), or run any UI program with
the environment variable ATF_UI_SCREENSHOT=shot.bmp.

**Constants**

- `WHITE = 0xFFFFFFFF`
- `BLACK = 0xFF000000`
- `TRANSPARENT = 0`
- `UNSET = -999999`

**Types**

```text
enum Align { Start, Center, End, Stretch }
```

```text
enum Justify { Start, Center, End, Between, Around, Evenly }
```

```text
enum Cursor { Default, Pointer, Text, Move, NotAllowed, ResizeH, ResizeV }
```

A rectangle you draw yourself. Coordinates are pixels (at 100% scale) from its top left corner. canvas(|c| { c.rect(0, 0, c.w, c.h, WHITE); c.circle(50, 50, 20, RED) }).size(200, 120)

```text
struct Canvas {
    ox: int
    oy: int
    w: int
    h: int
}
```


**Functions**

- `fn rgb(r: int, g: int, b: int) -> int` - opaque color from red, green, blue (0..255): rgb(37, 99, 235)
- `fn rgba(r: int, g: int, b: int, a: float) -> int` - color with opacity a from 0.0 (invisible) to 1.0 (opaque), like CSS: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.25)
- `fn hex(s: str) -> int` - CSS color text: "#rgb", "#rrggbb", "#rrggbbaa" or a name ("white", "tomato", "slate", ...)
- `fn mix(a: int, b: int, t: float) -> int` - the color between a and b: mix(a, b, 0.0) == a, mix(a, b, 1.0) == b
- `fn lighten(c: int, amount: float) -> int` - lighter / darker version of a color (amount 0.0 .. 1.0), keeping its opacity
- `fn darken(c: int, amount: float) -> int`
- `fn fade(c: int, a: float) -> int` - the same color with opacity a (0.0 .. 1.0): fade(BLACK, 0.2)
- `fn style() -> Style` - an empty style, to build a reusable set of properties: let card = style().bg(WHITE).radius(12)
- `fn column(children: [Node] = []) -> Node` - children one under the other (a vertical flex box)
- `fn box(children: [Node] = []) -> Node` - same as column
- `fn row(children: [Node] = []) -> Node` - children side by side (a horizontal flex box); they are centered vertically unless .align(..) says otherwise
- `fn stack(children: [Node] = []) -> Node` - children on top of each other, all in the same place (for layers, overlays, badges)
- `fn grid(cols: int, children: [Node] = []) -> Node` - a table of cols equal columns; children fill it row by row
- `fn scroll(children: [Node] = []) -> Node` - a column whose content scrolls with the mouse wheel when it is taller than the box
- `fn text(s: str) -> Node` - text; long text wraps at word boundaries, "\n" starts a new line
- `fn spacer() -> Node` - an empty element that takes the free space (pushes its neighbours apart)
- `fn divider() -> Node` - a thin line between items
- `fn button(label: str, on_click: fn()) -> Node` - a clickable button with a text label
- `fn textbox(value: str, on_input: fn(str)) -> Node` - a one-line text field: shows value, calls on_input(new value) when the user types
- `fn checkbox(checked: bool, label: str, on_change: fn(bool)) -> Node` - a check box with a label; on_change gets the new state
- `fn toggle(on: bool, on_change: fn(bool)) -> Node` - an on/off switch; on_change gets the new state
- `fn slider(value: float, on_change: fn(float)) -> Node` - a horizontal slider for a value from 0.0 to 1.0; on_change gets the new value while dragging
- `fn progress(value: float) -> Node` - a progress bar for a value from 0.0 to 1.0
- `fn image(path: str) -> Node` - a picture from a file (PNG, JPG, BMP, GIF); without a size it shows at its natural size. The picture fills the box and is cut to keep its proportions (CSS object-fit: cover).
- `fn textarea(value: str, on_input: fn(str)) -> Node` - a multi-line text field: shows value, calls on_input(new value) when the user types. Enter starts a new line, Tab inserts spaces; the arrow keys, Home/End, PageUp/PageDown, the mouse (click, drag, double click), Ctrl+A/C/X/V and Ctrl+Z/Y work. It is 5 lines tall unless .rows(n) or .height(..) say otherwise.
- `fn icon(name: str) -> Node` - a small picture from the symbol font that comes with Windows; give it a color and size like text: icon("save").font_size(20).color(hex("#2563eb")). A name that is not in the list is shown as it is, so icon("\u{E81E}") shows that symbol.
- `fn tabs(labels: [str], selected: int, on_select: fn(int)) -> Node` - a row of tab headers; selected is the number of the chosen tab, on_select(i) runs when one is clicked. The program shows the content of the chosen tab itself, below this row.
- `fn menu(items: [Node]) -> Node` - the list of choices in a menu; use it as the second argument of dropdown
- `fn menu_item(label: str, on_click: fn()) -> Node` - one line of a menu; the menu closes after it is clicked
- `fn dropdown(trigger: Node, content: Node) -> Node` - shows content (usually a menu) in a floating layer under trigger while the trigger has been clicked. A click anywhere else, or Esc, closes it. The result takes the place of trigger in the layout.
- `fn menu_button(label: str, items: [Node]) -> Node` - a text button that opens a menu: menu_button("File", [menu_item("Open", open), menu_item("Save", save)])
- `fn menu_bar(menus: [Node]) -> Node` - a bar of menu buttons across the top of a window; it is white, change that with .bg(..) and .color(..)
- `fn select(value: str, options: [str], on_change: fn(str)) -> Node` - a choice from a list: shows the chosen value; on_change(option) runs when another one is clicked
- `fn modal(content: Node, on_close: fn()) -> Node` - content on a dimmed layer over the whole window; on_close runs when the dimmed area is clicked or Esc is pressed. Add it last: root.add(modal(..)), or put it in the list of a stack.
- `fn dialog(title: str, body: Node, buttons: [Node], on_close: fn()) -> Node` - a modal card with a title, a body and a row of buttons on the right
- `fn canvas(draw: fn(Canvas)) -> Node` - an element that you draw with draw(canvas) each time the screen is drawn. Give it a size: .size(300, 200) or .grow()
- `fn focus_field(key: str)` - give the keyboard focus to the text field marked with .key(name) and put the caret at its end; does nothing when there is no such field. Handy in a shortcut: ui_shortcut("ctrl+f", || focus_field("search"))
- `fn ui_refresh()` - ask for the view to be rebuilt and the window to be redrawn (after changing data outside an event)
- `fn ui_quit()` - close the window (ui_run returns)
- `fn ui_title(title: str)` - change the window title
- `fn ui_every(ms: int, f: fn())` - run f every ms milliseconds while the window is open; the view is rebuilt after each call
- `fn ui_mouse_move(x: int, y: int)` - move the mouse pointer to (x, y) without clicking: hover styles and tooltips react (use it in tests)
- `fn ui_shortcut(combo: str, f: fn())` - Run f when the key combination is pressed anywhere in the window: ui_shortcut("ctrl+s", save). Modifiers: ctrl, shift, alt. Keys: a-z, 0-9, f1-f12, enter, esc, tab, space, delete, backspace, home, end, pageup, pagedown, left, right, up, down. A key without ctrl or alt (like "delete") does nothing while the user is typing in a text field. Registering the same combination again replaces the first one, so it can be called from the view function.
- `fn clipboard_get() -> str` - text on the Windows clipboard
- `fn clipboard_set(s: str)`
- `fn message_box(title: str, message: str)` - show a message and wait for OK
- `fn confirm_box(title: str, question: str) -> bool` - ask a yes/no question; true when the user answered Yes
- `fn open_file_dialog(title: str = "Open", filter: str = "All files|*.*") -> str?` - The Windows "Open" dialog. filter is pairs of name|pattern: "Text files|*.txt|All files|*.*". Returns the chosen path, or nil when the user cancelled.
- `fn save_file_dialog(title: str = "Save as", filter: str = "All files|*.*", ext: str = "") -> str?` - The Windows "Save as" dialog; ext (like "txt") is added when the user types a name without one. Returns the chosen path, or nil when the user cancelled.
- `fn ui_run(title: str, width: int, height: int, view: fn() -> Node)` - Open a window and show view() in it until the window is closed. width and height are the size of the inside of the window. view runs again after every click, key press and timer, so it should build the screen from the program's data each time. With the environment variable ATF_UI_SCREENSHOT=picture.bmp set, no window opens: the first frame is saved to that file instead (for tests and documentation of any UI program).
- `fn ui_headless(view: fn() -> Node, width: int, height: int)` - Start view() in a width x height area without opening a window and forget all earlier state (focus, open menus, scroll positions, undo). Then send events with ui_click, ui_type and ui_keypress, check the program's own data, and draw the result with ui_screenshot. Dialogs do not open while testing: message_box does nothing, confirm_box answers ui_answers' yes, the file dialogs return its path (nil when it is empty), and the clipboard is private to the program.
- `fn ui_answers(yes: bool, path: str)` - what the dialogs answer while testing: yes for confirm_box, and the path the file dialogs return ("" = cancel)
- `fn ui_last_dialog() -> str` - the text of the last message_box or confirm_box
- `fn ui_click(x: int, y: int)` - move the mouse to (x, y), press and release the left button
- `fn ui_drag(x1: int, y1: int, x2: int, y2: int)` - press the left button at (x1, y1), move to (x2, y2) and release it (selecting text, dragging a slider)
- `fn ui_type(s: str)` - type text into the focused field
- `fn ui_keypress(combo: str) -> bool` - press a key or combination: ui_keypress("enter"), ui_keypress("ctrl+a"), ui_keypress("shift+left"). Returns false when the key name is not known.
- `fn ui_click_text(s: str) -> bool` - click the middle of the first element that shows exactly this text (a button's label, for example); false when none is on the screen. Open menus and dialogs are searched first.
- `fn ui_screenshot(view: fn() -> Node, width: int, height: int, path: str, hover_x: int = -1, hover_y: int = -1) -> bool` - Draw view() into a picture file (.bmp) of width x height pixels without opening a window (for tests, documentation and thumbnails). hover_x, hover_y: optional mouse position to show hover styles.

**Methods of `Style`**

- `.width(v: int) -> Style`
- `.height(v: int) -> Style`
- `.size(w: int, h: int) -> Style`
- `.min_width(v: int) -> Style`
- `.max_width(v: int) -> Style`
- `.min_height(v: int) -> Style`
- `.max_height(v: int) -> Style`
- `.width_pct(p: float) -> Style` - width as a percentage of the parent's inner width
- `.height_pct(p: float) -> Style`
- `.padding(a: int, b: int = UNSET, c: int = UNSET, d: int = UNSET) -> Style`
- `.margin(a: int, b: int = UNSET, c: int = UNSET, d: int = UNSET) -> Style`
- `.gap(v: int) -> Style`
- `.align(a: Align) -> Style` - cross-axis placement of the children (CSS align-items)
- `.justify(j: Justify) -> Style` - main-axis distribution of the children (CSS justify-content)
- `.center() -> Style` - children in the middle on both axes
- `.wrap() -> Style` - a row that continues on the next line when it is full (CSS flex-wrap)
- `.rtl() -> Style` - right-to-left: rows start on the right and text aligns right (Hebrew, Arabic)
- `.bg(c: int) -> Style`
- `.gradient(from: int, to: int, angle: float = 180.0) -> Style` - linear gradient; angle in degrees like CSS (180 = top to bottom, 90 = left to right)
- `.border(w: int, c: int) -> Style`
- `.border_color(c: int) -> Style`
- `.radius(a: int, b: int = UNSET, c: int = UNSET, d: int = UNSET) -> Style` - corner radius: 1 value for all corners, or (top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left)
- `.pill() -> Style` - fully rounded ends (a pill or a circle)
- `.shadow(x: int, y: int, blur: int, c: int, spread: int = 0) -> Style` - drop shadow (CSS box-shadow): offset x, y, blur radius, color, spread
- `.opacity(o: float) -> Style`
- `.clip() -> Style` - cut the children at the edges of the box
- `.color(c: int) -> Style`
- `.font_size(v: int) -> Style`
- `.weight(w: int) -> Style` - 100 (thin) .. 400 (normal) .. 700 (bold) .. 900 (black)
- `.bold() -> Style`
- `.italic() -> Style`
- `.underline() -> Style`
- `.family(f: str) -> Style`
- `.text_align(a: Align) -> Style`
- `.line_height(f: float) -> Style` - line height as a multiple of the font size (1.5 = one and a half)
- `.nowrap() -> Style` - keep text on one line
- `.cursor(c: Cursor) -> Style`
- `.hover(h: Style) -> Style` - extra properties while the mouse is over the element (CSS :hover)
- `.pressed(h: Style) -> Style` - extra properties while the mouse button is held on the element (CSS :active)
- `.focused(h: Style) -> Style` - extra properties while a text box has the keyboard (CSS :focus)
- `.transition(ms: int) -> Style` - animate color changes (background, text, border) over ms milliseconds
- `.absolute(left: int = UNSET, top: int = UNSET, right: int = UNSET, bottom: int = UNSET) -> Style` - take the element out of the flow and place it relative to its parent's box (CSS position: absolute)
- `.merge(o: Style) -> Style` - this style with the properties set in o on top

**Methods of `Node`**

- `.style(st: Style) -> Node` - add the properties of a reusable style
- `.on_click(f: fn()) -> Node` - run f when the element is clicked (the view is rebuilt afterwards)
- `.on_drag(f: fn(float)) -> Node` - while the mouse is pressed on the element: f(position 0.0 .. 1.0 across its width)
- `.on_submit(f: fn()) -> Node` - text box: f runs when Enter is pressed
- `.placeholder(s: str) -> Node` - text box: grey text shown while it is empty
- `.password() -> Node` - text box: show dots instead of the letters
- `.key(k: str) -> Node` - a stable name, so the element keeps its state (focus, scroll) when the list around it changes
- `.add(c: Node) -> Node` - add one more child
- `.rows(k: int) -> Node` - text area: how many lines tall it is at first (default 5)
- `.on_pointer(f: fn(int, int)) -> Node` - canvas: f(x, y) runs when the mouse is pressed on the element and while it moves with the button down; x and y are measured from the top left corner of the element
- `.tooltip(s: str) -> Node` - show a small note under the element while the mouse is over it

**Methods of `Canvas`**

- `.clear(c: int)` - fill the whole canvas with a color
- `.rect(x: int, y: int, w: int, h: int, c: int)`
- `.rrect(x: int, y: int, w: int, h: int, r: int, c: int)` - rectangle with rounded corners
- `.outline(x: int, y: int, w: int, h: int, r: int, bw: int, c: int)` - only the border of a rectangle (bw pixels wide)
- `.circle(cx: int, cy: int, r: int, c: int)`
- `.ring(cx: int, cy: int, r: int, bw: int, c: int)` - only the border of a circle
- `.line(x1: int, y1: int, x2: int, y2: int, width: int, c: int)` - a straight line with round ends, width pixels thick
- `.text(x: int, y: int, s: str, c: int, size: int = 15, bold: bool = false)` - one line of text with its top left corner at (x, y)
- `.text_width(s: str, size: int = 15, bold: bool = false) -> int` - the width text would take
- `.pixels(x: int, y: int, w: int, h: int, pix: [int], pw: int, ph: int)` - Draw a picture from an array of 0xRRGGBB ints (pw * ph pixels, row by row), stretched to w x h pixels with the nearest pixel. Much faster than one rect per pixel: use it for software rendered scenes.
- `.pixels_smooth(x: int, y: int, w: int, h: int, pix: [int], pw: int, ph: int)` - The same as pixels, but the picture is scaled smoothly (bilinear filtering) instead of showing square blocks. Use it for software rendered scenes drawn at a low resolution: the game does not look pixelated.

## std/url

Web addresses: taking them apart, building them, and percent-encoding text.

```text
import "std/url"

let u = url_parse("https://ada@example.com:8080/a/b.html?x=1&y=two#top").unwrap()
println(u.scheme, u.host, u.port, u.path)       // https example.com 8080 /a/b.html
println(u.param("y") ?? "none")                  // two
println(url_encode("a b&c"))                     // a%20b%26c
println(url_query_build({"q": "x y", "n": "1"})) // q=x%20y&n=1
```

`port` is -1 when the address has none. `query` and `fragment` are kept without the ? and #.
Text is bytes in a str, so non-ASCII letters are encoded as UTF-8 bytes (%D7%A9 and so on).

**Constants**

- `URL_HEX_DIGITS = "0123456789ABCDEF"`

**Types**

```text
struct Url {
    scheme: str = ""
    user: str = ""
    host: str = ""
    port: int = -1
    path: str = ""
    query: str = ""
    fragment: str = ""
}
```


**Functions**

- `fn url_is_unreserved(c: byte) -> bool`
- `fn url_encode(s: str, plus: bool = false) -> str` - Percent-encodes s: letters, digits and - _ . ~ stay, every other byte becomes %XX. With plus: true a space becomes + (the form of a query string) instead of %20.
- `fn url_hex_value(c: byte) -> int`
- `fn url_decode(s: str, plus: bool = false) -> Result<str, str>` - Undoes url_encode. With plus: true a + becomes a space. A bad %XX gives an Err.
- `fn url_query_parse(q: str) -> {str: str}` - "a=1&b=two" -> {"a": "1", "b": "two"}. Names and values are decoded; a name without = gets "". When a name repeats, the last value wins.
- `fn url_query_build(m: {str: str}) -> str` - {"a": "1", "b": "x y"} -> "a=1&b=x%20y" (in the map's order)
- `fn url_valid_scheme(s: str) -> bool`
- `fn url_parse(text: str) -> Result<Url, str>` - Takes an address apart. A relative reference ("/a/b?x=1", "b.html") parses too, with an empty scheme and host.
- `fn url_path_normalize(path: str) -> str`
- `fn url_join(base: str, reference: str) -> Result<str, str>` - Resolves a reference against a base address, the way a browser follows a link: url_join("http://a.com/x/y.html", "../z") == "http://a.com/z"

**Methods of `Url`**

- `.param(name: str) -> str?` - the value of one query parameter, or nil
- `.params() -> {str: str}` - all query parameters as a map
- `.to_str() -> str` - the address as text again
- `.request_target() -> str` - the part to put after GET in a request: path and query ("/" when the path is empty)
- `.effective_port() -> int` - the port to connect to: the written one, or the default of the scheme (80, 443, 21, 22)

## std/xml

Read and write XML.

```text
import "std/xml"

let doc = xml_parse("<list><item id=\"1\">apple</item><item id=\"2\">pear</item></list>").unwrap()
for it in doc.children_named("item") { println(it.attr("id") ?? "?", it.inner_text()) }
let note = xml_element("note").set_attr("lang", "en").add(xml_text("hi & bye"))
println(xml_stringify(note))          // <note lang="en">hi &amp; bye</note>
```

A node is an element (a tag with attributes and children) or a piece of text (tag "").
Comments, the <?xml ...?> declaration and <!DOCTYPE ...> are skipped; CDATA becomes text.
Text made only of white space between elements is dropped; other text is kept as it is.

**Types**

```text
struct XmlNode {
    tag: str                 // "" for a text node
    attrs: {str: str}
    children: [XmlNode]
    text: str                // the text of a text node
}
```

```text
struct XmlParser {
    src: str
    pos: int
    err: str
}
```


**Functions**

- `fn xml_element(tag: str) -> XmlNode` - a new element with no attributes and no children
- `fn xml_text(text: str) -> XmlNode` - a new text node
- `fn xml_collect(n: XmlNode, tag: str, out: [XmlNode])`
- `fn xml_text_into(n: XmlNode, sb: StrBuilder)`
- `fn xml_escape(s: str, quote: bool = false) -> str` - replaces & < > (and " when quote is true) with entities
- `fn xml_write(sb: StrBuilder, n: XmlNode, indent: int, level: int)`
- `fn xml_stringify(n: XmlNode, indent: int = 0, declaration: bool = false) -> str` - the XML text of a node; indent > 0 puts each child element on its own line
- `fn xml_is_space(b: byte) -> bool`
- `fn xml_is_name_byte(b: byte) -> bool`
- `fn xml_add_utf8(sb: StrBuilder, cp: int)`
- `fn xml_parse(text: str) -> Result<XmlNode, str>` - reads an XML document and returns its root element; the error says the line
- `fn xml_read_file(path: str) -> Result<XmlNode, str>` - reads and parses an XML file
- `fn xml_write_file(path: str, n: XmlNode, indent: int = 2) -> bool` - writes a node to a file with the <?xml ...?> declaration; true on success

**Methods of `XmlNode`**

- `.is_text() -> bool` - true for a text node
- `.attr(name: str) -> str?` - the value of an attribute, nil when it is missing
- `.attr_or(name: str, default: str) -> str` - the value of an attribute, or the default when it is missing
- `.set_attr(name: str, value: str) -> XmlNode` - sets an attribute and returns the node, so calls can be chained
- `.add(child: XmlNode) -> XmlNode` - adds a child and returns this node, so calls can be chained
- `.add_text(tag: str, text: str) -> XmlNode` - adds the child <tag>text</tag> and returns this node
- `.elements() -> [XmlNode]` - the child elements (text nodes left out)
- `.child(tag: str) -> XmlNode?` - the first child element with this tag, nil when there is none
- `.children_named(tag: str) -> [XmlNode]` - the child elements with this tag
- `.find_all(tag: str) -> [XmlNode]` - every element below this one (at any depth) with this tag, in document order
- `.query(path: str) -> XmlNode?` - follows a path of child tags, like "server/port"; nil when a step is missing
- `.inner_text() -> str` - all the text inside this node, joined
- `.to_str() -> str`

**Methods of `XmlParser`**

- `.line() -> int`
- `.fail(msg: str)`
- `.at_end() -> bool`
- `.cur() -> byte`
- `.starts(s: str) -> bool`
- `.skip_ws()`
- `.skip_until(end: str) -> bool` - moves past the next `end`; false when it is missing
- `.skip_misc() -> bool` - skips white space, comments, <?...?> and <!DOCTYPE ...>; false on an error
- `.name() -> str`
- `.decode(raw: str) -> str` - replaces the entities in raw text
- `.element() -> XmlNode?` - reads an element; the position is at its '<'
